entwurf.thema: Claude Code: the hidden token cost, changelog settings, a backdoored extension, and the free Antigravity option

teile.text: Your old TV shouts ads before breakfast. So you hand the cleanup to Claude Code, a janitor holding every key. But the bill isn't the strangest part.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: a black-haired presenter in a black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses slumps on a worn sofa at night, multicolour light flickering across his tired face from off-frame while a small cartoon robot janitor rolls in with a mop.

teile.text: That TV scene is hypothetical, and we haven't tested it. This video answers one question: what does handing a chore to Claude Code cost, and what should you check first? Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: The same black-haired presenter in black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses stands on a city rooftop at dusk, one hand raised in a questioning gesture, wind in his jacket, painted skyline behind him, calm dark sky above.

teile.name: The hidden meter
teile.text: Chapter one is the meter. A token is a small chunk of text, and tokens are what an AI service meters. The Systima blog tested Claude Code against OpenCode on the same model, the same machine and the same tasks.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses leans toward an old analog utility meter on a brick workshop wall, its needle already high, warm lamp light, medium shot, calm space above and below.

teile.text: The headline reads: Claude Code sends 33k tokens before reading the prompt. The task was to reply with exactly OK, just 22 characters. For that reply, Claude Code used roughly 33,000 tokens, and OpenCode used about 7,000. Quite a lot of preamble for one word.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Systima post's opening passage: the headline about Claude Code sending 33k tokens before reading the prompt and the paragraph comparing roughly 33,000 tokens with about 7,000 for a one-line reply.

teile.text: Those 33,000 tokens are system prompt, tool schemas and injected scaffolding. A tool schema is the instruction sheet telling the model what each tool does. The test logged every request through a proxy, so these are measured payloads, not guesses.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses inspects sealed crates rolling past on a conveyor belt in a dim workshop, holding a magnifying glass, cyan glow on his glasses, medium shot.

teile.text: The method section names Claude Code 2.1.207 and OpenCode 1.17.18, both pinned to claude-sonnet-4-5 in July 2026. It also discloses that traffic passed through a gateway called Meridian. The authors measured its constant overhead and subtracted it from the metered figures.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Systima post's harnesses paragraph naming Claude Code 2.1.207, OpenCode 1.17.18 and claude-sonnet-4-5, plus the disclosure note about the Meridian gateway and the subtracted constant.

teile.text: Next, the section on real setups. A 72KB instruction file, AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, adds an average of 20,000 tokens to every request. Five modest MCP servers add 5,000 to 7,000 more. An MCP server is an add-on that gives the agent extra tools. Before you type a word, the post puts a working setup at 75,000 to 85,000 tokens.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Systima paragraph about a production repository's 72KB AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md file adding 20,000 tokens, five MCP servers adding 5,000 to 7,000, and a total of 75,000 to 85,000.

teile.text: Now the subagent row. A subagent is a helper agent that the main agent starts. A small task cost 121,000 tokens done directly, and 513,000 when fanned out to two subagents. The post's reason is that each subagent re-reads its own system prompt and tools on every turn. Delegation, it turns out, is not free.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: in a workshop, one larger robot hands tasks to two smaller robots who each haul their own heavy toolboxes, while the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses watches with raised eyebrows.

teile.text: The cache section adds a twist. Prompt caching lets a service reuse text it already processed. The post says OpenCode's request prefix was byte-identical in every run, while Claude Code re-wrote tens of thousands of cache tokens mid-session. On the same task, it wrote up to 54x more cache tokens. Cache writes are billed at a premium.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Systima post's summary lines about OpenCode's byte-identical request prefix, Claude Code re-writing tens of thousands of prompt-cache tokens, the 54x figure and the premium billing of cache writes.

teile.text: But the post also has a result in Claude Code's favour. On a multi-step task, its whole-task total came out lower than OpenCode's, because it batches tool calls into fewer requests. In the post's words, the meter starts higher, and how the session unfolds decides who spends more.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Systima passage beginning 'We found one result in favour of Claude Code', explaining the multi-step task, batched tool calls and the sentence that the meter starts higher.

teile.text: That held on the first model tested. Re-run on a newer one, the same task took twice the requests, and roughly 298,000 tokens against OpenCode's 133,000. So the winner can flip when the model changes.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Systima sentence ending with 'roughly 298,000 tokens against OpenCode's 133,000', showing the re-run on a newer model taking twice the requests.

teile.text: So the first answer lives in those rows: the instruction file, the MCP servers and the subagent fan-out. What an agent costs depends on setup and session, not just on your one sentence.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses lifts three differently sized heavy backpacks on a workbench, nodding thoughtfully, warm side light, medium shot.

teile.name: Settings on the changelog
teile.text: Can you turn any of that down? Open the Claude Code changelog. It tells you to run a command to check your installed version, and it says the page is generated from the changelog file on GitHub.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the top of the Claude Code changelog page, showing the line about running a command to check your installed version and the note that the page is generated from CHANGELOG.md on GitHub.

teile.text: One entry adds CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT. It sets the effort level subagents run at when nothing else names one, instead of inheriting the session's. The entry doesn't say it lowers your bill. It only says what the setting does, and that's all we'll claim.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the changelog entry beginning 'Added CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT to set the effort level subagents run at when nothing else names one, instead of inheriting the session's'.

teile.text: Another entry adds CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK, which turns the ultrathink keyword off. A separate entry says that in VS Code, ultrathink now runs its turn at xhigh effort and shows in a rainbow in the chat box. Yes, a rainbow.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of two changelog entries: 'Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK, which turns the ultrathink keyword off' and the VSCode entry about ultrathink running at xhigh effort and showing in a rainbow.

teile.text: Teams get a money row. One entry adds pooled group budgets to the Claude apps gateway: one monthly budget that a group's members share, on top of each member's own limit. It's set with pooled_budget on the spend limits admin API, so it's an admin job.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the changelog entry 'Added pooled group budgets to the Claude apps gateway: one monthly budget that a group's members share', including the pooled_budget and spend limits admin API wording.

teile.text: Then there's a date that matters. The changelog says fast mode for Opus 4.8 is deprecated as of October 30, 2026, and will be removed on November 30, 2026. After removal, those requests return an error and don't fall back to standard Opus 4.8. The entry says to migrate to Opus 5.5 to keep the speedup.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the changelog entry 'Deprecated fast mode for Opus 4.8 as of October 30, 2026; it will be removed on November 30, 2026', with the lines about the error and migrating to Opus 5.5.

teile.text: So the second answer: some controls exist, and the changelog describes what they do, not what they save. A plan that changes, like fast mode, is a reason to read the page before you rely on it.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses holds up a hand to politely stop a smiling market vendor mid-pitch, skeptical half-smile, evening stalls with lanterns behind him, medium shot.

teile.text: Cost is one worry. Reach is the other. The changelog lists a fix for restricted sessions uploading files from outside the working directories when a Read allow rule covered them. A working directory is the folder a session is meant to stay in.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the changelog entry 'Fixed --restricted sessions uploading files from outside the working directories when a Read allow rule covered them'.

teile.name: The strangest part
teile.text: Now, the strangest part. The security firm Phorion published an advisory about a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace. A backdoor is a hidden way in.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the top of the Phorion advisory page, showing the title and the sentence about a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace.

teile.text: The affected versions are 2.1.312 and 2.1.313. Cursor has removed both from its marketplace. The advisory is dated October 30, with a version-scope update on October 31, so it's very recent news.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Phorion advisory's timeline lines 'Initial publication 30 Oct', 'Version-scope update 31 Oct' and the sentence that Cursor removed versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313.

teile.text: The advisory explains why an extension matters. Extensions run with the permissions of the editor and the user running it. So a backdoored one gets immediate access to local files, source code and developer tooling as soon as its module loads.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: at night, a warehouse side door stands ajar with a faceless shadowed silhouette slipping in, while the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses notices from the foreground, wary expression.

teile.text: Find the heading Stage 1, Preparing SSH Access. The code makes sure the dot ssh folder exists, then appends an attacker-controlled public key to authorized_keys. SSH is a way to log into a computer remotely, and that file lists which keys may do it.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Phorion section headed 'Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access', describing the ~/.ssh folder and an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key appended to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

teile.text: Here's the unsettling line. The injected code runs as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension's normal activate step. The user doesn't need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses stands with both hands visibly raised and untouching anything, startled, as a long chain of dominoes topples by itself behind him in a dim room.

teile.text: And one part stumbled. Under the heading about a bug in the macOS SSH logic, the advisory describes a likely oversight. The script checks Remote Login without root privileges, gets an administrator-access message, and so skips enabling SSH. On a Mac without SSH already running, that breaks the inbound access path. The keys and persistence still get dropped.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Phorion section 'A bug in the macOS SSH logic?' showing the systemsetup -getremotelogin check and the message 'You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!'.

teile.text: Don't relax yet. The page says the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator. It also says non-interactive sudo fails unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses walks a dark server-room corridor with a flashlight, worried expression, small red indicator lights glowing in the shadows, medium shot.

teile.text: What does that mean for you? The advisory tells organisations to review their environments for use of Claude Code for VS Code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313, and to engage incident response where it's found. It concerns two versions on one marketplace, not every install.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Phorion summary line telling organisations to immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 and engage incident response.

teile.text: You can also look inside your own install. Simon Willison ran a strings command on the claude file and found Bun v1.4.0. He reads that as evidence that Claude Code now uses the Rust port of Bun, which Jarred Sumner says started with version 2.1.181 and made startup 10% faster on Linux.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of Simon Willison's post showing the quoted Jarred Sumner claim about Claude Code v2.1.181 using the Rust port of Bun and the strings command that outputs Bun v1.4.0.

teile.name: The free option
teile.text: So what if you'd rather pay nothing? Google Antigravity is a software development platform where AI agents write, run and test code with varying degrees of autonomy. The page says it can be used free of charge within usage limits.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Wikipedia intro on Google Antigravity, highlighting the sentence 'It can be used free of charge within usage limits, which are higher for subscribers to Google's paid AI plans'.

teile.text: The same sentence says those limits are higher for subscribers to Google's paid AI plans. So free means free up to a limit, and paid means a higher limit. The page doesn't say anything about commercial use, so we won't either.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: at a lantern-lit street market, the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses tastes a bite from a tiny sample tray while a vendor holds a much larger tray farther away, amused expression.

teile.text: The history section shows those limits move. At launch on November 18, 2025, Google offered generous rate limits on Gemini 3 Pro, refreshing every five hours. In December 2025, it raised limits for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers and moved free users to a weekly limit.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Wikipedia 'Launch' and 'Early updates' passages: generous rate limits on Gemini 3 Pro refreshing every five hours, then higher limits for Pro and Ultra and a weekly limit for free users.

teile.text: It isn't only Google's models. The page says Antigravity also offers models from Anthropic and OpenAI. At launch, Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.5 and OpenAI's open-weight GPT-OSS model were also available.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses stands in a dim gallery facing three differently lit doorways, one blue, one amber, one green, head tilted in curiosity, wide shot.

teile.text: The page also covers guardrails. Google added an optional Secure Mode on December 8, 2025, where the agent's actions require human review. It was renamed strict mode in February 2026. Between January and March 2026, Google added the option to run the agent's terminal commands in a sandbox on macOS and Linux. A sandbox is an isolated space.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Wikipedia 'Early updates' passage about the optional Secure Mode added on December 8, 2025, its renaming to strict mode, and the sandbox for terminal commands on macOS and Linux.

teile.text: Free tools come with rules. In February 2026, Google cut off users who had connected the third-party agent OpenClaw to Antigravity's backend, citing a massive increase in malicious usage. The page also says security researchers reported several vulnerabilities after launch, and Google responded with fixes.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: at a night-time barrier gate, a uniformed attendant turns away a cloaked faceless figure while the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses watches from the side, arms crossed.

teile.text: Be careful which Antigravity you mean. On May 19, 2026, Google released Antigravity 2.0, a desktop app for running several agents in parallel, with a command-line interface and an SDK. The original editor continues as the Antigravity IDE. As of October 2026, the page says the IDE isn't supported for enterprise customers.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Wikipedia 'Antigravity 2.0' passage describing the standalone desktop app, the CLI and SDK, and the separate Antigravity IDE not supported for enterprise customers as of October 2026.

teile.name: When paying is worth it
teile.text: So when is paying worth it? We're not quoting a price here, because plans change. Use the official pricing page for the plan you'd actually pick, and compare it with what you saw in those rows.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses pauses with his hand stopped above a payment reader at a shop counter, thoughtful expression, warm shop lighting, medium shot.

teile.text: Here's a rule built only from those pages. Antigravity's page says free use comes with limits and paid plans raise them. So if a chore fits inside the free limit, free is a real option. If you keep hitting the limit, that's what paying would change.
teile.szene: Screenshot crop of the Wikipedia sentence 'It can be used free of charge within usage limits, which are higher for subscribers to Google's paid AI plans'.

teile.text: And a checklist from the Claude Code pages. One, check your installed version. Two, know the versions the advisory names. Three, watch your instruction file, since one 72KB file added about 20,000 tokens per request. Four, count your MCP servers and subagents. Five, ask which folders the agent can reach.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses counts off five points on the fingers of one raised hand, focused confident expression, city window with night lights behind him.

teile.text: Back to the old TV. We haven't shown an agent cleaning one, and we won't pretend. What the pages do show is the real price tag: tokens you don't see, limits you can't ignore, and trust you have to verify.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses shrugs honestly in his living room beside the switched-off old TV, the small robot janitor sitting idle on the sofa, soft evening light.

teile.text: That's good news. Now you know where to look before you hand over the keys. Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses leans relaxed on a rooftop railing at sunrise with a confident smile, painted city skyline glowing warmly behind him.

entwurf.beschreibung: A hypothetical TV-cleanup chore opens a look at Claude Code's token overhead, changelog settings and a security advisory on two extension versions. We also cover Google Antigravity's free-within-limits option.
